claims.text: Quantitative Input Influence (QII) measures capture the degree of causal influence of inputs on outputs of decision-making systems.
Causal QII measures account for correlated inputs while measuring influence.
QII measures quantify the joint influence of a set of inputs on decision outcomes.
The average marginal influence of an individual input within a set is computed using aggregation measures such as the Shapley value.
A number of QII-based transparency reports can be made differentially private with minimal noise addition.
QII is efficiently approximable in the evaluated scenarios.

evidence.description: The authors introduce a family of Quantitative Input Influence (QII) measures that capture the degree of influence of inputs on outputs of systems.
Distinctively, our causal QII measures carefully account for correlated inputs while measuring influence.
The QII measures also quantify the joint influence of a set of inputs (e.g., age and income) on outcomes.
The average marginal influence of the input is computed using principled aggregation measures, such as the Shapley value.
The authors prove that a number of useful transparency reports can be made differentially private with very little addition of noise.
The authors show that in the situations considered, QII is efficiently approximable.

methodologies.name: Quantitative Input Influence (QII)
methodologies.description: A causal framework that quantifies input influence on machine learning outputs, handling joint influence, marginal influence via Shapley values, and differential privacy.
conditions: black box access to the learning system

limitations.text: Decision-making processes of algorithmic learning systems are often opaque, making it difficult to explain why a specific decision was made.
QII measures require black box access to the learning system to serve as a transparency mechanism.
